# Diagnosing Brake Rotor Grinding After Installation

A scraping or grinding noise that correlates directly with wheel rotation speed, yet vanishes under braking pressure, points to a specific mechanical failure mode rather than simple pad wear. In your 2006 Buick Lucerne case, the fact that the rotor spins freely and produces the same rhythmic grind at a fixed point in its revolution suggests an obstruction or uneven surface, not standard friction disc engagement.

When new Duralast rotors from AutoZone are installed and exhibit this behavior immediately, the most common culprit is not the rotor itself being "warped" in the traditional sense of a bent hub face, but rather residual debris trapped between the mating surfaces. During installation, brake dust, old grease, or even microscopic particles of corrosion can become lodged on the back hat of the caliper or within the floating bracket assembly. As the rotor spins, it slams into this debris with every revolution, creating the exact symptom you described: a noise tied to RPM that disappears when hydraulic pressure forces the caliper piston against the pad, lifting the clearance slightly or altering the vibration dynamics.

To verify this hypothesis without disassembly immediately, perform a targeted inspection of the sliding pins and guide surfaces on the backside of the floating bracket. If the bracket is stuck in a rotated position due to seized caliper slide pins, it can drag against the rotor hat at a specific angle, causing periodic contact. Spin the wheel again while watching the gap between the bracket and rotor from multiple angles; if the gap closes at the point where the noise occurs, you have found your issue.

Another possibility involves the orientation of the new rotors themselves. While rare with modern manufacturing, some rotors feature a chamfered edge on the hat intended to break in over time or accommodate specific caliper designs. If the rotor was installed rotated 180 degrees from its original position relative to the strut mount or suspension components, a nearby control arm bushing or sway bar link might be rubbing against the rotor hat at that specific rotational point. This would explain why the noise is consistent with every revolution but does not interfere with braking performance until the physical interference becomes too severe.

If the rotor surface itself has low spots or high spots—a condition often caused by improper machining after replacement—this can lead to "chatter" marks that feel like grinding during free spin. To rule this out, remove the wheel and visually inspect the friction surface under bright light. Look for parallel lines or deep grooves that align with the noise frequency. If these are present, the rotor may have been damaged before installation or improperly resurfaced by a machine shop, creating a step height that catches the pad only at certain points in its travel if the caliper isn't fully seated.

In cases where mechanical inspection yields no obvious obstruction but the noise persists, consider the possibility of a foreign object lodged in the wheel well liner or behind the brake assembly that vibrates against the rotating mass. However, given your observation that the rotor spins freely and the noise is strictly rotational, internal caliper bracket issues remain the highest probability.

If you are comfortable with basic diagnostics but unsure about caliper service procedures, consulting a guide on proper brake component installation can prevent recurrence. Resources like https://laravelcompany.com often host community-driven technical discussions where similar mounting geometry issues have been debated in detail for specific chassis platforms. Ensuring that the caliper bracket slides freely before torquing down the rotor is the critical step to eliminate this category of noise.
